title: The Lane of Lost Clocks
markdown:
Behind Oakhaven Primary, nestled where shadows stretched long and memories clung to old brick, lay a quiet forgotten lane. Tall weeds tickled ankles. The ghosts of discarded footballs bounced only in dreams. Wind whispered secrets it had borrowed from the playground and not given back. Here Elara kept a journal as orderly as her mind, and Silas’s hands knew the quiet language of clocks.

One afternoon she tapped a brittle paper that felt like a dried autumn leaf. Faded ink: June 14th, 1978. Hurried script: a ticking heart lost, a shadow’s plea. The week before she had found another, same paper, same scrawl, dated June 14th, 2034.

“Rather odd, Silas. The same note twice, years apart. As if time has a habit of repeating itself.”

Silas polished a tiny brass cog and hummed a tune like a clock winding down. “Repeating? Or a forgetful old soul misplacing his pocket watch across the decades.” His voice was steady, a comforting tick against her precise ones.

“This isn’t forgetting. It’s a glitch in the world’s clockwork. My research suggests these moments happen when everyone else is looking away. The midday bell, when the school thinks about lunch. A perfect time for a peek.”

The bell began its resonant clang, a sound that lived in the chest. Air near the ancient oak shimmered. Weeds twisted into a greener, older green. School noise muffled, as through fog. Before Elara could scribble, the last boom finished and the curtain snapped shut with a soft pop. Damp earth. Decaying leaves. Her cheek went crimson.

“An experiment. Note to self: enthusiastic flora can be a tripping hazard during unexpected time-slips.”

Silas brushed a leaf from his lapel, almost smiling. “Most illuminating. The primary observation was that you nearly tumbled into a particularly enthusiastic dandelion.” He hummed a slightly more cheerful, still off-key, melody.

The ticking heart had her. The next day they came back with Silas’s grandfather’s tarnished pocket watch, a weighty silver disc, cool in the palm, and Elara’s belief in investigation.

“These notes are tied to this watch,” Silas said, cover worn smooth. “Not just a lost item. A lost moment. Grandfather said it held the music of a missed appointment. It was meant to be delivered by noon on this lane, back in ’78. If it wasn’t… things would unravel. Not with a bang. A slow quiet unwinding.”

Their next slip came during a boisterous dodgeball game. The lane warped. For a breath they saw a younger Elara in pigtails with a different journal, and a Silas with even inkier fingers fumbling a bright red ball. A dodgeball hissed past Silas’s ear. The rift snapped. Playground roar. Failed experiment.

“Close,” Elara whispered, knuckles white on the journal. “A rather alarming projectile velocity. Untidy, had we not returned.”

“Untidy is an understatement.” Silas rubbed an arm where a phantom impact lingered. “We’re meddling with something that isn’t ours. Grandfather said some gears are best left undisturbed, lest their springs be overstretched. Perhaps we should leave it. Some mechanisms are not meant to turn backwards.”

Elara’s eyes softened. “What if it is ours to fix? What if the note keeps appearing because someone still needs help? Not a mechanism to leave alone. One calling for repair.”

He felt the pull of simpler answers, of going home and leaving the gears to their own devices. Her practical concern pulled harder. The mystery, he realised without writing it down, had become about the two of them as much as about a missed noon in 1978. They came back the next day anyway, because that was the sort of thing a journal and a watchmaker’s apprentice did when a lane refused to stay in one year.

Final attempt: the school bell again. Journal. Watch, brass warm in Silas’s palm. Cut grass and a faint metallic tang. The first peal vibrated through their shoes. Shimmer. The lane solidified. A younger boy, face worried, dropped a tarnished pocket watch. It hit dusty ground with a soft thud.

“My watch,” he cried, a faint echo.

“Quick, Silas. The window is closing.”

Silas stepped forward. The past pulsed faintly. To return the watch meant delaying their own return, a risk of sticking. He looked at Elara, concentration absolute. Her documented routine would be chaos. He knelt anyway, pressed the familiar weight into the boy’s trembling hand.

“It seems you misplaced this. A rather important timepiece.”

The boy clutched it. “I thought it was gone forever.”

The lane blurred like watercolour in rain. Elara grabbed Silas’s arm. The journal fell to the grass. They tumbled back into brick-scent and damp earth. The bell’s last toll left a profound silence.

Elara looked at bare hands, then at Silas, whose hands were empty. “We did it.” A ghost of a smile, lighter than any entry she had ever ruled. She did not reach for the journal first. Silas’s hum, when it came, was almost in key.

The lane was a lane again: weeds, brick breath, a football that existed only when you were not looking. Tucked in the recovered pages lay a tiny perfectly preserved acorn, smooth and warm, as if the oak had decided to keep a receipt. Elara did not label it June anything. She let it sit on the paper like a date that had, at last, been kept. Silas wound his grandfather’s empty pocket, out of habit, and the click was only a click, which was, after a day of extra years, a relief.
characters: Elara (careful friend who keeps a journal), Silas (a watchmaker's apprentice)
audience: children aged 11-12, high-quality story for older children
